study.title: Matthew 7 - Discernment, prayer, fruit and true obedience
study.overview: Matthew 7 concludes the Sermon on the Mount with a series of very practical warnings and invitations. Jesus teaches his disciples to abandon hypocritical judgment, to treat sacred things with discernment, to pray with persevering confidence, to live according to the rule of love for others, to choose the narrow way, to recognize false prophets by the fruits and to obey his words in fact. The chapter ends with the reaction of the multitudes: they were amazed because Jesus taught with his own authority, not like the scribes. The focus of the chapter is not only to listen to Jesus, but to answer him with obedient faith and transformed life.

outline.title: Don't judge hypocrisy, but deal with yourself first
outline.explanation: Jesus forbids condemnatory and partial judgment, especially when a person ignores a greater sin in himself. The image of the cisco and the beam is exaggerated on purpose to show the incoherence of correcting the other without personal repentance. The goal is not to eliminate all moral evaluation, but to prevent the proud and cruel stance that arises above others.

outline.title: Discernment, persevering prayer and the golden rule
outline.explanation: Not everything must be exposed indiscriminately: there are holy things that are not to be delivered to those who will despise them. Then Jesus encourages insistent prayer, presenting the Father as someone more willing to give good gifts than ordinary human parents. The passage culminates in the golden rule, which summarizes the Law and the Prophets: to do to others what one desires to receive from them.

outline.title: The narrow door and the test of false prophets
outline.explanation: Entering the narrow door is to follow Jesus in a real way, not just nominal, knowing that there is a contrast between the wide path of perdition and the tight path of life. Then Jesus warns against false prophets, who look like sheep, but they are wolves from the inside. The criterion of recognition is the fruit: the good tree produces good fruit; the evil, bad fruit; and the one that produces no good fruit is judged.

outline.title: True Obedience and the Authority of Jesus
outline.explanation: Not every verbal confession of faith guarantees entry into the Kingdom; it is necessary to do the Father's will. Even impressive religious acts, such as prophecies and wonders, do not replace obedience. Jesus closes with the parable of the two houses: to hear and to practice his words is to build on the rock; to hear without practicing is to build on the sand. The chapter ends by highlighting the unique authority of the teaching of Jesus, which surprises the crowds.

study.context: The notes show that this chapter is the closure of the Sermon on the Mount. Jesus speaks to his disciples, but there are also crowds listening. The environment is that of a public teaching in which its authority is compared to that of the scribes; the difference, according to the notes, is that the scribes depended on quotations and traditions, while Jesus taught with direct authority.
study.theology: Matthew 7 unites grace, truth, and obedience. First, Jesus confronts religious hypocrisy: the problem is not only to err in judgment, but to judge without personal repentance. Then he shows that persevering prayer is born of trust in the heavenly Father, who gives good things to those who ask. The chapter also teaches that the ethics of the Kingdom is summed up in loving others concretely, not only in affirming principles. The narrow door indicates that following Jesus requires a real and exclusive decision; there is no neutral way. The image of the tree and the fruits teaches that spiritual authenticity is revealed in the visible result of life, not in appearance. Finally, the passage of those who say "Lord," says that verbal profession, gifts and religious activities do not replace the will of the Father. The authority of Jesus is not only didactic; it requires an answer. Listening without practicing is spiritual foolishness.

scholarViews.insight: Jesus closes the Sermon on the Mount calling his listeners to decide for him and his teaching; the narrow door represents the decision to follow him as Messiah, and there is no half-term to follow him and reject him.

The conclusion of the chapter shows the indispensable need for obedience to the commandments of Christ; it is not enough external profession of religion, practical correspondence with the Father's will is needed.
Jesus finished the sermon, and the people marveled because he taught with royal authority; his doctrine was convincingly, different from the teaching of the scribes.

questions: In which areas of my life do I try to correct others before I examine my own sin seriously?
Is my life showing fruits consistent with the faith I confess, or just religious appearance?
Have I heard the words of Jesus as information, or as an authority that should be obeyed?
study.practice: This week, choose a situation where you often judge someone hardly and replace that attitude with personal examination, prayer and a humble conversation. Also practice the golden rule in a concrete way: intentionally do something good for someone who cannot easily repay. When reading the Sermon on the Mount, ask not only what Jesus said?, but what will I obey today?."
study.uncertainty: The notes do not detail all possible historical connections, so the context was limited to what they explicitly affirm: conclusion of the Sermon on the Mount, presence of disciples and multitudes, and contrast between Jesus and the scribes. In the image of the fruits and the narrow door, there are confessional interpretations in the notes; they were presented as interpretive reading, not as absolute statements beyond the text. Also no technical senses of original terms were added, as the notes do not provide them.
